item.title: When Jealousy Protects Love
item.description:
Jealousy

When Jealousy Protects Love

A balanced dose of jealousy can help maintain intimacy and trust.

Posted July 18, 2026

Key points
  • The need to belong is a fundamental human motivation.
  • Moderate jealousy can protect a relationship's unique significance.
  • Romantic uniqueness does not always require strict exclusivity.
Source: Anna Pou / Pexels

"Never make a decision when you are upset, sad, jealous, or in love."—Mario Teguh

Jealousy has a bad reputation, but eliminating it entirely may not be desirable. Romantic relationships flourish not only because they satisfy our need to belong, but also because they provide a sense of unique significance.

Lovers do not want to be merely another person in their partner's life; they want to occupy a distinctive place. At its core, romantic jealousy is often less about preventing a partner from interacting with others than about preserving the unique place one occupies in the partner's world. Jealousy functions as a psychological mechanism for protecting what makes a relationship special.

But when does jealousy strengthen love, and when does it undermine it?

The Need to Belong

"You belong to me."—Bob Dylan

"You don't own me. Don't say I can't go with other boys."—Lesley Gore

According to Roy Baumeister and Mark Leary, belongingness is a fundamental human need. It involves frequent positive interactions with the same people within a stable framework of mutual care and commitment. Although many people are attracted to the excitement of multiple romantic partners, the need for an enduring, caring relationship is more fundamental than the attraction to multiple partners. A sense of belonging is essential for psychological well-being, whereas a lack of belonging is associated with poorer health, lower happiness, and reduced psychological adjustment (Baumeister & Leary, 1995; Allen et al., 2022).

Romantic belonging grows through meaningful experiences that partners share; it cannot arise from private feelings alone. Belongingness is expressed not only through shared experiences but also through sensitivity to threats to the relationship. The hope of building intimacy and the fear of losing it are two sides of the same emotional coin. In this sense, jealousy often reflects not insecurity alone, but the value we place on a cherished relationship.

Yet belonging alone is not enough. Lovers usually seek not merely connection, but a connection that is uniquely theirs.

The Need for Uniqueness

"I like jealous men. I love jealousy. I do."—Adriana Lima

People often describe romantic relationships as both unique and exclusive, but these are not identical qualities. Uniqueness refers to the distinctive nature of the romantic bond itself, whereas exclusivity refers to limiting others' access to that bond. Uniqueness concerns the relationship's intrinsic value; exclusivity is one way of protecting it. The popular notion of a soulmate illustrates the value of uniqueness. Although romantic non-exclusivity can weaken uniqueness, it does not necessarily eliminate it. Many couples view exclusivity as a safeguard for preserving the distinctive character of their bond.

Exclusivity itself exists in many forms and degrees. Some people seek complete emotional and sexual exclusiveness. Others accept emotional intimacy with someone else while viewing sexual infidelity as a serious violation. Still others negotiate specific exceptions without believing that the core relationship has been compromised. The boundaries differ across couples, but the underlying goal remains the same: protecting the relationship's distinctive place.

The distinction between uniqueness and exclusivity becomes especially clear in the case of a widow who continues to love her deceased husband while deeply loving a new partner. The new relationship may be unique without requiring the erasure of the previous one. Uniqueness, therefore, need not depend upon being the only significant love. Similarly, even in successful polyamorous relationships, partners often seek reassurance that their relationship remains unique in some respect—whether through shared history, emotional intimacy, particular commitments, or future plans. The persistence of jealousy in these relationships suggests that the desire for uniqueness survives even when exclusivity is relaxed.

The Nature of Romantic Jealousy

"It's hard to know another's lips will kiss you."—Hank Williams

Romantic jealousy is a response to the possibility of losing an important relationship to someone else. Unlike envy, which involves two people and feelings of undeserved inferiority, jealousy is inherently triangular: It involves the fear that another person may replace us (Kristjánsson, 2024).

Jealousy arises when a partner's relationship with someone else threatens either the exclusivity of the bond or its unique place in the partners' lives. The perceived threat may involve losing the relationship altogether or merely losing its privileged place in a partner's world. We suffer not only because we may lose someone we love, but also because such a loss raises uncomfortable questions about our own worth and replaceability. This helps explain why jealousy is often one of the most intense emotions in romantic life (Ben-Ze'ev, 2000; 2019).

Jealousy also feeds on imagination. Marcel Proust described it as "a historian without documents." People often become jealous not because of actual infidelity but because a partner directs attention, affection, or emotional support elsewhere. Even when suspicions are unfounded, jealousy may persist because imagination readily fills the gaps in our knowledge.

One particularly destructive form is retroactive jealousy. Here, people reinterpret a partner's past through the lens of the present relationship, negatively judging actions that occurred long before the couple met. Such jealousy reflects a kind of retrospective ownership over a partner's past. Persistent rumination about previous relationships rarely strengthens the present relationship and often weakens it.

Evolutionary psychologists have emphasized jealousy's role in mate guarding and reproductive success. While this perspective explains why jealousy evolved, it does not fully explain why even secure, committed partners continue to experience mild jealousy. A complementary view is that jealousy helps preserve the relationship's unique significance.

Is Romantic Jealousy Valuable?

"Jealousy can even be good for love. One partner may feel secretly flattered when the other is mildly jealous."—Helen Fisher

Romantic jealousy can serve an important psychological function: protecting what makes a valued relationship matter to us. Yet, like many human emotions, its value depends largely on its intensity. Jealousy is neither inherently virtuous nor inherently harmful. Its presence even among people in polyamorous and open relationships suggests that the desire to protect valued relationships extends beyond monogamy.

Like physical pain, jealousy is adaptive in moderation. The complete absence of pain may indicate that something important is wrong, whereas chronic pain becomes a problem in itself. Similarly, mild jealousy reminds us that the relationship matters; overwhelming jealousy can damage the very relationship it seeks to protect. Healthy jealousy signals that we value the relationship. Excessive jealousy, however, shifts from protecting love to controlling one's partner.

Flourishing relationships require trust more than suspicion, yet trust does not require emotional indifference. Seeking belonging and a sense of unique significance is both natural and valuable. The challenge is to keep jealousy proportionate—strong enough to protect what is precious, yet restrained enough to preserve the trust, respect, and freedom on which enduring love depends.

item.title: Baby Boomers’ Keen Interest in Genealogy
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

Baby Boomers’ Keen Interest in Genealogy

Personal Perspective: The desire to leave a legacy is a developmental task.

Posted July 18, 2026

Key points
  • Baby Boomers pursue genealogy to fulfill a deep need to leave a meaningful legacy.
  • The findings from genealogical research often lead to bewilderment that are often both positive and negative.
  • Lessons learned from genealogy are often painful reminders of the human condition.

Genealogy is one of the top hobbies for older Americans, with 70 percent of Baby Boomers valuing this knowledge.

According to the Pew Research Center, the generation of post-war babies in 1964 included around 72.5 million people, but is projected to be around 1 million in 2062.

Baby Boomers born between 1946 and 1964 who are approaching or have reached retirement have curiosity and goals specific to this phase of their lives. These goals include leaving a legacy, understanding their roots, and preserving their family stories.

The Erickson model of development described the eighth and final stage of life as “ego integrity versus despair.” Life review is an effective method to navigate these diametrically opposite polarities.

New Orleans and Family Connections

Growing up in New Orleans, we have always had close-knit families, and we were proud of our multiple ethnicities. I knew my maternal and paternal grandparents and spent quality time with them regularly. I learned from an early age about discrimination, segregation, and “separate but equal” from my daily environment, such as the Catholic school and health care institutions.

There was an occasional mention of “generations” before my grandparents, even though we had roots dating back to the 18th century in the city and state on both the maternal and paternal sides of the family.

What I Learned About My Family

On one visit home to see my mom, I discovered a brown, crumpled newspaper clipping and a large sepia photo of a grand gentleman. The fragile paper article was from the local paper dated 1913.

After putting the pieces together, I saw the article told the story of my second great-grandfather, Charles Joseph Montaldo, who was born between 1838 and 1841.

No one in the family ever mentioned his name or his life. This entire side of our lineage was excluded from our history. As a child, my mom was close with and regularly visited one of my great-grandfather Charles’ daughters, Aunt Eva, and spent time with this relative.

"Genealogy Roadshow"

I learned that PBS' Genealogy Roadshow was filming in New Orleans and chose to apply to participate. Surprisingly, after two Zoom sessions, they chose my second great-grandfather as one of the unique individuals from New Orleans.

Charles was a local politician in New Orleans and was engaged in the civil rights of African Americans. The Times Picayune, published on Friday, September 4, 1874, contained a complaint about Charles in his official role as State Supervisor of the Third Ward.

article continues after advertisement

This racist story demonstrates the prejudice of their "enlightened" attitude about newly enfranchised African American citizens. In an attack on Charles Montaldo's credentials as a voter registrar, they implied much but proved nothing, even having to admit his correctness. This sort of prejudice focused on Charles and other white "scalawags" and skewed the reporting to villainize them as traitors to the "lost cause."

The complaint centered around the number of "Negroes" who registered to vote.

"The Negroes, as usual, have rushed to the registration office in patriotic anxiety to enroll their names! The whites are far behind, and seem to show little zeal and energy, as yet. Of the 780 persons registered in the Third Ward, about three Negroes or more to every white man" [abbreviated content].

Election to the Louisiana Legislature

In 1872, Charles was elected to the Louisiana State Legislature. Four years later, during his reelection bid for his seat in the legislature, he was accused of vote rigging. The events were reported in the local papers.

The reelection campaign to the Louisiana Legislature was influenced by white supremacists from Mississippi because of his history of registering Black Americans to vote after Reconstruction in New Orleans. In 1877, Charles was running the Gaiety Theater in downtown New Orleans.

In 1876, after his failed attempt at a second term in the Louisiana Legislature, Charles returned to New Orleans and held various jobs. Charles left New Orleans in 1880 and headed west to search for gold in the Klondike area of Canada.

In the 1885 census of Colorado, Charles can be found living in San Miguel County, Colorado, working as a saloon keeper.

Where Was Charles?

The last communication the family received from Charles was a postcard he mailed to his daughter Eva on November 16, 1890. The postcard was mailed from Fair Haven, Washington. The photo of Charles on the postcard was taken by Dobbs & Fleming photo studio on Holly Street in Sehome, Washington.

article continues after advertisement

In the 1900 census, Ida Montaldo lived in Dayton, Columbia, Washington State, with her parents. The record stated that she had been married for seven years with no children.

On June 12, 1900, Charles was enumerated with other passengers aboard the Steamer Aberdeen in Nome, Alaska. This was at the height of the Nome Gold Rush. No documents were found placing Charles in the Klondike.

The End of a Complicated Life

Charles was buried in Reno, Nevada, and passed on May 2, 1910. Afterwards, the news eventually spread to New Orleans in the newspapers.

"Relatives of Charles A. J. Montaldo (Once a Prominent New Orleanian) Learn of His Demise in the Faraway West." Along with a professional photo was a lead story in the Daily Picayune in 1913, telling the story of this once-famous man.

Another article published in 1913: "Soldier of Fortune Succumbs After Long Regarded Dead: Charles Montaldo Is Once King of Sporting World Here and a Picturesque Figure in Local Politics."

Genealogy Results Are Both Positive and Negative

This aspect of his life clearly caused a major and profound scandal with the family, the city, and the local Catholic Church. In that historical period, the belief system of Catholicism stated that the individual would have been living in a constant state of manifest sin; they were barred from confession, Holy Communion, and receiving last rites upon death.

Lessons learned from genealogy are often painful reminders of the human condition. However, a human life is complicated, and each person has free will. My great-great-grandfather may have believed in equality, fairness, and social justice; however, he was clearly breaking the laws of the United States and the Catholic Church.
